title: Adaptive concurrency/backoff shims and ergonomic streaming examples for embeddings + rerank SDKs
creator: Emily Park
description:
Goal: deliver cross-language (Python/TypeScript/Go) helpers and example patterns that provide ergonomic streaming APIs for embeddings and rerank endpoints while adding an adaptive concurrency and backoff shim that preserves latency SLOs and reduces token cost on bursty workloads.

Deliverables:
- SDK helper libraries: lightweight concurrency controller + backoff strategy pluggable per-client.
- Streaming ergonomics: idiomatic async/iterator helpers (Python AsyncGenerator + sync iterator fallback, TS AsyncIterable + backpressure semantics, Go context-aware streaming client).
- Pagination/batching utilities: single-call helpers that auto-chunk inputs to target token budgets, yield partial progress, and expose resume tokens.
- Cross-sdk parity checklist & examples demonstrating identical behavior across languages for: retry rules, max_in_flight, per-request token budgets, and resume token format.
- Tests: integration harness against runtime staging with synthetic prefix-cache hit ratios and KV pressure to validate behavior.

Motivation/Context: Existing SDKs have divergent streaming ergonomics and retry defaults (see ENG-423999 and ENG-32781). That causes customer confusion when migrating examples between languages and leads to subtle cost regressions under bursty loads. This ticket unifies the developer experience and introduces an adaptive concurrency controller that uses three signals: tail latency samples, KV cache hit fraction, and active batch queue depth, to decide aggressive vs conservative concurrency settings.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Python, TS, and Go SDKs expose a BackoffController/ConcurrencyShim with same config keys and documented defaults.
2) Example repo contains a streaming rerank example in all three languages that resumes from a resume_token and handles partial batches.
3) Integration tests show <=10% P95 latency increase at 99th percentile throughput compared to current aggressive defaults, and 20-30% token-cost savings for cache-friendly traffic patterns.
4) Docs + migration guide published to Confluence.
5) PRs merged and a canary release published to npm/pypi/goreleases.
